reasons: The usage check gives a clear message.
A missing .env file is accepted silently.

terms.meaning: A named setting that a program reads when it starts.
A plain text file of setting names and values kept outside the code.
A program started by another program, here the command being wrapped.
A message sent to a running program, such as a request to stop.
A number a program returns when it ends. Zero usually means success.

depends_on: The .env file at the repo root (optional).
used_by: Root package.json commands dev, db:schema and db:seed.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Reading the .env file
sections.what: Finds the .env file at the repo root and reads it if it exists.
sections.why: Keeps settings in one file outside the code.
sections.watch_out: If the file is missing, the command runs with no file values, and the gap may only show up later.

sections.name: env, child exit handler
sections.title: Running the wrapped command
sections.what: Merges the settings so shell values win. Requires a command to be given, runs it with the terminal attached, forwards stop signals to it, and passes its exit status back.
sections.why: Lets wrapped commands behave as if they were run directly, including responding to Ctrl+C.
sections.watch_out: On Windows the command goes through a shell, which can change how arguments with spaces are read.

summary: Runs any command with the values from the repo-root .env file loaded, while values already set in the shell take priority.
purpose: Lets local commands read secrets and settings from a file without the developer exporting each one by hand.
why: The header states that shell values override the .env file.
how: Finds the .env file at the repo root and parses it if it exists. It merges the file values with the current environment, letting shell values win. It takes the command and its arguments from the command line, runs them with the merged settings, passes stop signals through, and returns the same exit status.
inputs: The .env file at the repo root, and the command and arguments given on the command line.
outputs: The command's own output on the same terminal, and its exit code or stop signal.
risks: The .env file holds secrets. If it is missing, the script carries on silently, so missing settings only appear later. On Windows the command runs through a shell, which can change how arguments with spaces are read.
debug: If a variable seems missing, check that it is in .env and that the shell is not setting it to a different value. If the command is not found, check its spelling. If the usage message appears, no command was given.
